summary: Reviewed the dvpwa aiohttp application: DAO layer (SQL access), views/routes, auth utilities, middlewares, app setup, Jinja2 templates and config. The app is intentionally vulnerable: it contains a classic SQL injection in student creation, stored XSS enabled by globally disabling template auto-escaping, a disabled CSRF middleware, weak MD5 password hashing, non-HttpOnly session cookies, and missing server-side authorization on state-changing endpoints. Overall risk is critical; the SQLi and XSS are reachable by unauthenticated users. Coverage was the full Python source and templates; static JS/CSS assets and SQL schema were only skimmed.

findings.title: SQL injection in Student.create via string-formatted INSERT
findings.description: Student.create builds the INSERT statement by Python %-formatting the raw `name` into the SQL string instead of passing it as a bound parameter. The value comes straight from attacker-controlled POST data: views.students (sqli/views.py:57) calls Student.create(conn, data['name']) with no validation, and the /students/ POST route (sqli/routes.py:14) has no authentication, so any anonymous user can inject SQL. A payload in the `name` field (e.g. breaking out of the quoted VALUES and appending stacked statements or a subquery) executes with the app's full DB privileges, allowing data exfiltration (including users.pwd_hash) or modification.
findings.evidence: q = ("INSERT INTO students (name) " "VALUES ('%(name)s')" % {'name': name})  -> await cur.execute(q). Source: data['name'] from POST /students/ in views.py:55-57. Contrast with the safe parameterized queries elsewhere (e.g. Course.create uses cur.execute(q, {...})).
findings.recommendation: Use a parameterized query: cur.execute("INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES (%(name)s)", {'name': name}). Never interpolate user input into SQL text.

findings.title: Stored XSS enabled by disabling Jinja2 autoescape globally
findings.description: aiohttp_jinja2 is configured with autoescape=False, so no template output is HTML-escaped. User-controlled values are rendered directly into HTML, e.g. review.review_text in course.jinja2:22, course.title/description, and student.name in students.jinja2:16. Reviews can be created by unauthenticated users (POST /courses/{id}/review, views.py:111-131, no auth), so an attacker can store a <script> payload that executes in every visitor's browser (including an admin), enabling session hijacking and admin-action forgery.
findings.evidence: setup_jinja(app, loader=..., context_processors=[...], autoescape=False). Sink example: course.jinja2 line 22 `{{ review.review_text }}` rendered without escaping; review_text stored verbatim via Review.create (review.py:28-36).
findings.recommendation: Enable autoescaping (autoescape=True, the aiohttp_jinja2 default) and only mark explicitly-trusted content safe. Validate/encode user input.

findings.title: CSRF protection middleware disabled
findings.description: A working CSRF-token middleware exists (sqli/middlewares.py:25-38) and templates emit the token, but it is commented out of the application middleware list, so no POST request is checked for a CSRF token. All state-changing endpoints (login, create student, create course, create review, evaluate/grade, logout) accept forged cross-site POSTs. Combined with the missing per-handler auth checks, an attacker page can cause an authenticated admin's browser to perform privileged actions.
findings.evidence: middlewares=[session_middleware, # csrf_middleware, error_middleware]. The csrf_middleware that pops session['_csrf_token'] and compares to form data is defined but never registered.
findings.recommendation: Re-enable csrf_middleware in the middleware chain and ensure all forms submit the token (they already render csrf_token()).

findings.title: Missing server-side authorization on state-changing endpoints
findings.description: Access control is enforced only in templates (e.g. course.jinja2:41 shows the grading form only to admins), but the handlers perform no authorization. The evaluate handler, which records student marks (an admin-only action), has no @authorize decorator and is reachable by any anonymous client via POST /students/{id}/evaluate/{course_id}. The same gap applies to students (create student, views.py:51-60), courses (create course, views.py:83-93) and review (create review, views.py:111-131) — none check get_auth_user/authorize, so any unauthenticated user can create or modify data. Only logout uses @authorize.
findings.evidence: async def evaluate(request): ... await Mark.create(conn, student_id, course_id, data['points']) with no authorize() decorator; routes.py:21-23 maps POST to it unauthenticated. Compare logout (views.py:156) which does use @authorize().
findings.recommendation: Apply @authorize()/@authorize(ensure_admin=True) (sqli/utils/auth.py) to every state-changing handler per its required privilege level rather than relying on template-only checks.

findings.title: Passwords hashed with unsalted MD5
findings.description: User.check_password compares the stored hash to a plain unsalted MD5 of the password, and fixtures store md5(password) (migrations/001-fixtures.sql:10-13). MD5 is fast and unsalted, so if the users table is leaked (e.g. via the SQL injection above) passwords are trivially recovered with rainbow tables/brute force. Identical passwords also produce identical hashes.
findings.evidence: return self.pwd_hash == md5(password.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest(). Stored as md5('superadmin'), md5('password'), etc.
findings.recommendation: Use a slow, salted password hash such as bcrypt/scrypt/argon2 and compare with a constant-time verifier.

findings.title: Session cookie set without HttpOnly flag
findings.description: The Redis session storage is created with httponly=False, so the session cookie is accessible to client-side JavaScript. Together with the stored XSS enabled by autoescape=False, an injected script can read document.cookie and exfiltrate a victim's (including admin's) session, leading to full account takeover.
findings.recommendation: Remove the httponly override (default is True) and also set secure=True and an appropriate SameSite attribute for the session cookie.

findings.title: Application runs with debug mode enabled
findings.description: The aiohttp Application is constructed with debug=True and run.py configures logging at DEBUG level. In a production deployment this increases verbosity of error output and can leak internal details; it should not be hard-coded on.
findings.evidence: app = Application(debug=True, middlewares=[...]) and run.py:11 logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG).
findings.recommendation: Drive debug and log level from configuration/environment and default to non-debug in production.
